issue.title: Python and Rust flat query parsers build different AndExpr operand orders, so the parity suite cannot assert parse-AST equality
issue.description:
PROPOSED BY phase bead sase-s9.6 (epic sase-s9, "Procs tab query filtering") on
2026-08-23T13:38:31Z as a PROPOSED FOLLOW-UP, verified and routed here by that epic's
land agent (sase-s9.land).

NOT CAUSED BY sase-s9. That epic's `rust` phase added parity tests, and those tests are
what exposed this; the divergence itself predates the epic and reproduces on fields the
epic never touched (see the Stitches case in the reproduction).

The two implementations of the shared flat query grammar build different `AndExpr`
operand orders for the same multi-field input. Python's flat parser emits field terms in
compiled-profile order (effectively sorted by key), while the Rust flat parser in
`sase-core` emits them in first-seen clause order. Canonicalization already agrees, and
`AND` evaluation is order-independent, so no user-visible behavior differs today.

WHY IT STILL MATTERS: the stated contract for this grammar is that both implementations
are byte-identical, and the parity suite in
`tests/test_query_profile_corpus_facade.py` cannot assert parse-AST equality for any
multi-field query while this holds. That leaves a permanent hole in the exact test that
is supposed to catch future Python/Rust grammar drift, which is the whole reason the
`rust` mirror phase exists.

SCOPE: pick one order as canonical and make both parsers emit it, then extend the
parity parameters in `tests/test_query_profile_corpus_facade.py` to assert full
parse-AST equality (not just canonical-form equality) for multi-field queries.
Sorted-by-key is the likelier choice since Python already does it and the canonical
string is already sorted, but that is a call for whoever works this. The Rust half
lands in the linked `sase-core` repo (open it with `/sase_repo`); per
`docs/rust_backend.md` the release lane owns the `sase-core-rs` floor bump in this repo.

task_type_fields.impact:
## Impact

No user-visible effect today: canonical form matches, cache keys are keyed on the
canonical string, and `AND` evaluation is commutative.

The cost is to the safety net. `tests/test_query_profile_corpus_facade.py` is the
designated guard against Python/Rust flat-grammar drift, and it currently has to
compare canonical strings rather than parse ASTs for any query with more than one
field term. A future divergence in how one side builds its AST -- operand nesting,
negation placement, a dropped term -- would pass that suite as long as the canonical
strings happened to agree.
task_type_fields.repro:
## Reproduction

Verified at master HEAD 062ae22c2 in workspace sase_12 with sase-core-rs 0.31.7
installed (the release that contains sase-core commit aeefa36, the sase-s9.6 port).

```bash
.venv/bin/python - <<'EOF'
from sase.ace.query_profile import compile_query_profile
from sase.ace.query_profile.profiles import stitches_query_schema
from sase.ace.query.profile_reference import parse_query_for_profile
from sase.core import query_profile_corpus_facade as f

p = compile_query_profile(stitches_query_schema())
for q in ("repo:x author:y", "author:y repo:x"):
    py = parse_query_for_profile(q, p)
    rs = f._parse_artifact_query(q, p)
    print(q, "| EQUAL:", py == rs)
    print("   PY:", [o.key for o in py.operands])
    print("   RS:", [o.key for o in rs.operands])
EOF
```

Observed:

```
repo:x author:y | EQUAL: False
   PY: ['author', 'repo']
   RS: ['repo', 'author']
author:y repo:x | EQUAL: True
   PY: ['author', 'repo']
   RS: ['author', 'repo']
```

Equality holds only when the input happens to already be in the Python order. The
`procs` profile shows the same thing on the epic's own bound keys -- `min:30s max:2h`
gives Python `[max, min]` and Rust `[min, max]` -- while
`canonical_query_for_profile` returns `max:7200 min:30` for both, confirming the
divergence is confined to the parse AST.

Note the Stitches case uses `repo:`/`author:`, two long-standing fields with no
relationship to the bare-boolean or bound-key extensions, which is what establishes
that this predates epic sase-s9.
